implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to the same event-loop runtime as JavaScript, so the realization is the Promise: the start method returns Promise<T> immediately, async/await linearises the wait, and the eventual value is typed (Awaited<T>) so the result type is visible at the await site. Downlevel async functions mean the same source compiles to older targets, so the model is available regardless of the emitted syntax; the typing documents the runtime contract instead of changing it, and rejections still need runtime handling.
pitfalls: Types are erased: a Promise<Report> rejection is still an unhandled rejection at runtime unless a catch is attached - the type system never enforces handling.
catch (e) is unknown (useUnknownInCatchVariables) so it must be narrowed before use, and a typed payload says nothing about cancellation.
Promise<void> covers both fire-and-forget and 'wait for completion', which makes 'did anyone consume this result?' unverifiable from the type alone.

variants.name: Typed event map with template-literal event names
variants.idiom_name: Event-map interface + template-literal event names over addEventListener/EventEmitter
variants.implementation_notes: The event-shaped realization made safe by types: an event-map interface pairs each event name with its payload, and template-literal types (TypeScript 4.1) let libraries type names such as 'done'/'progress' so the completion payload is checked at the subscription site ('on listens on the event "firstNameChanged"'). Use it where several parties observe progress and completion or the API must stay EventTarget-compatible; the runtime guarantees remain the emitter's, so once-semantics and unsubscription stay the caller's job.
pitfalls: A typed listener signature does not make delivery single-shot: 'done' can still fire twice, and a listener registered after emission never runs.
Template-literal typing catches name typos at compile time but not missing unsubscription - listener leaks stay a runtime concern.
Handler types declared in method style are bivariant, so a listener accepting a narrower payload than the emitter sends compiles cleanly and fails only at runtime.
